# Cūḷaassapura Sutta (MN 40 (PTS MN i 281))

**ID:** MN 40 (PTS MN i 281)  
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Cūḷaassapura Sutta  
**PTS:** MN i 281  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul3.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul3.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cūḷaassapura Sutta* ("The Shorter Discourse at Assapura", MN 40) is the fortieth discourse in the *Majjhimanikāya* [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Delivered at Assapura, it functions as a companion piece to the preceding *Mahāassapura Sutta* (MN 39) [Humphreys 1956; Rogell 2003]. The sutta defines "the way proper to the recluse" (*samaṇa*), asserting that monastic designation and ascetic status are not earned merely through external trappings, formal requisites (such as wearing the patchwork robe), or external bodily austerities (such as nakedness or ceremonial bathing) [Durham 2004; Bronkhorst 1998; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Instead, genuine asceticism requires inward purification from unwholesome mental defilements, specifically including ill-will and other corruptions of the mind [Durham 2004; Anālayo; Rogell 2003]. When a practitioner observes freedom from these unwholesome states, gladness and joy arise, leading successively to bodily tranquility, happiness, and meditative concentration [Shaw 2006], with the text also incorporating the practice of the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995].

**Sources**

- [Shaw 2006] Sarah Shaw, Buddhist Meditation: An Anthology of Texts from the Pāli Canon (2006) — Extract describing the sequence from inner purification to gladness, joy, tranquility, happiness, and concentration
- [Humphreys 1956] Christmas Humphreys (ed.), Buddhist Students Manual (1956) — Note on the pairing of the great and small Assapura discourses on ascetic duties
- [Durham 2004] Jeffrey Sean Durham, Certainty's Seal: Dynamics of Religious Assurance in Indian Buddhism (2004) — Discussion of MN 40.6 on robes as outer marks versus inner moral purity
- [Cheung 2013] Cheung Tsui Lan Liza, Doctrines of Spiritual Praxis from Abhidharma to Mahāyāna Yogācāra (2013) — Comparison of ascetic praxis between the Assapura suttas and the Śrāvakabhūmi
- [Anālayo] Bhikkhu Anālayo, From Craving to Liberation: Excursions into the Thought-world of the Pali Discourses (1) — Role of overcoming ill-will as a mental corruption to be reckoned a true ascetic
- [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995] Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Middle Length Discourses of the Buddha (1995) — Sutta title, thematic summary regarding inner purification versus austerities, and reference to the brahmavihāras
- [Rogell 2003] Sharda Rogell, Pressing Out Pure Honey: A Practitioner's Study Guide (Majjhima Nikāya) (2003) — Summary of MN 40 as a continuation of MN 39 concerning inner purification from defilements
- [Bronkhorst 1998] Johannes Bronkhorst, The Two Sources of Indian Asceticism (1998) — Analysis of external ascetic practices (nakedness, ceremonial bathing) listed in MN 40 that do not constitute true asceticism
